title: Pudding: A Retargetable Compiler for Processing-Using-DRAM Systems
summary: Processing-Using-DRAM (PUD) architectures exploit the physics of DRAM arrays to perform Boolean operations directly in memory, eliminating the data movement bottleneck in memory-intensive workloads. Several PUD architectures have been recently proposed which differ in their primitive operation sets, row allocation models, and execution metrics. These architectural differences are today hard-coded in emerging PUD-aware compilers, making crossarchitecture reuse impossible. We present a retargetable, end-to-end compilation framework for PUD architectures. The central idea is to make the architecture description a first-class object in the compilation pipeline: retargeting to a new PUD architecture only requires supplying its description. Built upon the MLIR framework, our compiler operates at two coupled levels. At the tensor level, it lowers high-level programs through bit-slicing, mixed-precision assignment, and integer-linear-programming (ILP) based placement to reduce the number of PUD commands and inter-bank data movement. At the logic level, it employs equality saturation to explore Boolean network implementations, with rewrite rules and cost functions derived directly from the architecture description. Evaluated on representative workloads across multiple PUD targets with the same compiler passes, our framework matches (and in several cases surpasses) architecture-specific hand-optimized compilers, while delivering retargetability and extensibility.

title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
summary: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

title: HLWalk: Modal-Split Random-Walk Thermal Analysis for Heterogeneous 2.5D/3D ICs
summary: Efficient thermal analysis is essential for accelerating the design of 2.5D/3D ICs. However, existing random-walk thermal solvers can suffer from boundary discretization errors and high computational costs when resolving fine-scale structures such as through-silicon vias (TSVs). To address these challenges, we propose HLWalk, an efficient random-walk thermal solver for heterogeneous 2.5D/3D ICs. We introduce local boundary integral reconstruction to eliminate discretization errors in local-time-based boundary treatments. To accelerate boundary preprocessing, we employ modal splitting: low-order modes are computed deterministically, while Monte Carlo sampling estimates only the residual. We further develop scale-aware random-walk transport to efficiently resolve fine-scale structures without requiring fine discretization throughout the domain. Experiments on 2.5D/3D IC benchmarks show that HLWalk achieves remarkable wall-clock speedup and better accuracy across settings.

title: A Pipeline-Parallel System for Depth-Recurrent Models
summary: Depth-recurrent (Looped) models raise effective depth by applying a shared stack of blocks several times. Scaling them usually requires pipeline parallelism, but commonly used interleaved 1F1B is drawn for an acyclic stage graph in which each micro-batch enters each stage once. Once that stack is split across stages, the same stage is visited several times on one micro-batch and later stages feed earlier ones: native 1F1B has no slot for the extra visit, cannot rank a first iteration against a second, and its neighbour-only send/receive order has no back edge to the first stage, so the arrangement stalls or fires out of order. We present Loop-PP, which rebuilds both the timetable and the communication for this cyclic layout. It schedules different iterations of the same stage separately, specializes a 1F1B skeleton into a globally consistent order over those visits, and emits a static instruction stream per rank that separates posting from waiting so communication overlaps local compute. Loop-PP is bit-identical to a single-stage reference. On 8B-60B MoE models, it lowers peak memory by as much as 32.8\%, and with compute budget fixed, the best observed throughput rises by 12.7\%.

title: Verifiable Logical-Physical Contracts for Refactored On-Die Power Control Circuitry
summary: Recent literature allows independent hardware experiments to occupy a single die for scalable and cost-efficient silicon prototyping. Within this framework, specialized hardware functions including low-power control mechanisms can be offered as reusable on-die microservices. However, this requires well-defined contracts connecting digital requests to physical behavior. We present a checkable logical-physical contract formulation including a physical contract model describing service completion between client and provider through formally verified digital guarantees and physically validated completion conditions. We introduce Lightswitch, a proof-of-concept on-die power control microservice. We assess post-layout designs in TSMC 28nm and demonstrate how checkable contracts provide formal guarantees.

title: Torcalia.jl: An MPI-based Runtime System for Asynchronous Task Parallelism in Julia
summary:
Designed to address the two-language problem, the Julia programming language provides a powerful platform for developing high-performance scientific computing and machine learning applications. Such applications increasingly exhibit irregular, adaptive, or data-driven workloads for which traditional bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) models often struggle to efficiently exploit the available parallelism. Asynchronous many-task (AMT) runtime systems offer a compelling alternative, decomposing computations into fine-grained tasks that are dynamically scheduled across the hierarchical architecture of modern HPC systems.
  This paper introduces Torcalia$.$jl, a Julia package designed to orchestrate the asynchronous execution of tasks across both shared and distributed memory environments. Built on top of MPI$.$jl and Julia's native multithreading, Torcalia employs a dependency-aware task scheduling scheme that combines the work-sharing and work-stealing paradigms to achieve adaptive load balancing. Tasks can be nested arbitrarily, enabling applications to exploit multiple levels of parallelism, while application-level distributed shared memory (DSM) extends task-based shared-memory programming to multi-node clusters. Beyond task-based programming, the proposed library supports skeletal programming, providing high-level abstractions that facilitate the implementation of parallel applications at scale. Evaluated on the ARIS supercomputer using four diverse workloads, Torcalia demonstrates strong scalability, reducing wall-clock time by up to 18.1% compared with Dagger, a state-of-the-art task-based engine in Julia. The source code of Torcalia$.$jl is publicly available at https://github.com/CEID-HPCLAB/Torcalia.jl.

title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
summary: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

title: Which $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ Algorithm is Suitable for You? An Empirical Benchmark on Real Network Traces
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of OPODIS 2026
summary: Unreliable failure detectors (UFDs) are a fundamental abstraction for dependability and fault tolerance in distributed systems, supporting core distributed algorithms, such as consensus. Yet selecting a suitable detector remains difficult because existing implementations are evaluated under different environments, workloads, parameterizations, and quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We address this problem by systematizing 14 $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ and closely related $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$-style UFDs, implementing 13 of them, and providing a reusable benchmark for their empirical comparison. Our methodology evaluates detectors through common QoS metrics, such as detection time, mistake rate, and query accuracy, and combines same-input replay of network traces with live deployment for detectors whose active probing or cooperative behavior requires online execution. We then formalize failure-detector selection as a constrained algorithm-selection challenge, mapping operational requirements to suitable detector candidates. We instantiate this methodology under controlled variations of communication rate, host load, and crash regime. Applying the selection process shows that no detector is uniformly preferable across the evaluated settings. At relaxed detection-time budgets, 2W [Tomsic et al., IPDPS 2015] is the most frequently selected detector, appearing in 12 of 16 scenario-metric combinations for $T_D \le 500$ ms, whereas stricter budgets yield substantially more scenario- and metric-dependent selections. The benchmark and selection methodology provide a reusable basis for practical detector selection and for establishing stronger analytical baselines for future failure-detection approaches, including learning-based detectors.

title: A Systematic Method of GPU Verification on Subsystem Modelling
comment: 10 pages, 14 figures. Published in the Proceedings of DVCon China 2017
summary: ARM Fast Model is a software modelling system for simulating multiple systems IPs integrated in a subsystem. Fast Model allows customer to run whole software stack as early as system IPs' specification is just ready. In this paper, we talk about a systematic method to enable GPU modelling and make whole system software stacks executable for both CPU and GPU in the integrated modelling environment, and eventually the major GPU IP can be verified. With our solution, we can directly run commercial benchmarks like Antutu and GFX Bench in Android target system with underlying ARM Fast Model mobile subsystem support. This was unbelievable in the past due to 3D rendering simulation for GPU verification is very slow. We also introduce some special techniques to improve performance. Eventually the whole software stack can directly work on real hardware without any changes as soon as the first tape-out is ready.

title: X-BQSR: Holistic Acceleration of Base Quality Recalibration for Scalable Genomic Analysis
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Author's submitted version (preprint) of paper accepted at Euro-Par 2026 (European Conference on Parallel Processing). E. Marinelli and I. D. Kabadzhov contributed equally. The final authenticated version is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-35248-4_36
summary:
With the continued decline in sequencing costs, genomics-based precision medicine is gaining increasing importance. The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) is the standard framework for converting raw genomic data into actionable variants, but one of its most expensive steps is base quality score recalibration (BQSR), which corrects systematic sequencing errors. Despite significant work on accelerating other parts of the variant calling pipeline, BQSR has not been systematically explored on GPUs.
  In this work, we analyze BQSR to identify computational and I/O bottlenecks and show that simply offloading key stages to an accelerator is insufficient to achieve overall gains. We then present X-BQSR, a holistic redesign of the entire BQSR pipeline, including I/O, compression, and kernel execution, to better leverage GPU parallelism. We implement X-BQSR using portable SYCL kernels for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, along with native CUDA and HIP backends for comparison, and we evaluate its performance against previous FPGA work. Our evaluation shows up to 141.7x acceleration compared to standard GATK and 8.7x acceleration compared to a proprietary GPU-accelerated solution.

title: CXL Coherence Writes Back What Surviving Hosts See, Leaving Flushes Only for Ordering
summary: Hosts that share memory over Compute Express Link (CXL) cache its lines, and a host that crashes loses the lines it has modified and not written back. Designs for such memory stop every host when one crashes, assume stored energy, or flush after each operation. We show that when a crashing host's clients die with it, the flushes a host crash requires are those that keep one line from reaching the memory device before a line it depends on, and not those that make a finished operation durable. The reason is a property that CXL requires of the fabric: a modified line is written back before another host accesses it. Whatever a surviving host has seen is then on the device, and our crash condition lets a crash drop operations that only the crashed host observed. We prove the claim for operations that take effect in a single store, and test it on small instances of models of three published designs, whose operations store several times. A lock table needs no flush to keep the locks of surviving hosts. A persistent hash index keeps every operation a survivor has observed, and in two workloads it writes fewer than half as many lines to the device as its published code does. An allocator's flush of each new reference is neither sufficient nor necessary for the survivors' safety: the allocator lacks ordering flushes, one of them when a reference changes hands.

title: Decoupling Faults from Uncertainty: Message-Efficient Byzantine Agreement with Local Predictions
comment: 29 pages. To appear in OPODIS 2026. Full version with complete proofs
summary:
Byzantine Agreement protocols are traditionally designed under worst-case uncertainty about which processes are faulty, coupling the adversary's corruption budget $t$ with the system's epistemic uncertainty. Recent work showed that auxiliary failure predictions can improve round complexity, but cannot improve communication complexity when prediction errors are unconstrained. In this paper, we initiate a theoretical study of the complementary question: how much can Byzantine Agreement benefit when each process is guaranteed a local bound on its prediction error?
  We study this question through the local $k$-error prediction model, in which each process receives a local classification vector differing from the ground truth in at most $k$ positions. The predictions need not be common, and honest processes may hold substantially different views about whom to trust.
  Under this promise model -- where correctness relies on the local error bound holding -- we present a synchronous Byzantine Agreement algorithm requiring $n \ge t + 4k + 1$, where $n$ is the total number of processes, $t$ is the maximum number of failures, and $k$ is the local error bound per honest process. In the regime where local uncertainty is small ($k \ll t$), our protocol decouples communication from the total fault budget $t$: in an execution where the actual maximum prediction error is $s \le k$ and the actual number of failures is $f \le t$, the protocol terminates in $O(s+1)$ rounds and sends $O((f+k)ks + nk)$ honest messages, achieving $o(n^2)$ communication when $t = Θ(n)$ and $k = o(\sqrt{n})$. Finally, we show that it is not possible to solve Byzantine Agreement in the local $k$-error prediction model with fewer than $Ω(nk)$ honest messages.

Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

title: HiPerfCC-KVCache: Accelerating Confidential LLM Serving with Hierarchical KV Caching
summary: Hierarchical key-value (KV) caching reduces repeated prefill computation in large language model serving by retaining reusable state beyond GPU memory. Under GPU confidential computing (CC), however, protected transfers can erase this benefit. We show that bulk KV copies hold driver locks during prolonged CPU-side processing, stalling independent serving operations despite separate threads and streams. Our characterization on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs shows how lock scope, copy granularity, and allocation ownership affect foreground progress and transfer parallelism. Guided by these findings, we present HiPerfCC-KVCache, which manages resource lifetimes, prioritizes ready token readback between bounded backup submissions, and parallelizes KV restores through auxiliary contexts with shared GPU staging. Implemented in SGLang, HiPerfCC-KVCache uses existing protected transfer interfaces without hardware or driver changes. Across three models and three workloads on H200, HiPerfCC-KVCache achieves a geometric-mean output-token throughput speedup of $1.74\times$ (up to $2.72\times$) over the staged KV-transfer HiCache-Workers baseline at the highest tested loads. Mean time to first token decreases by 36% on average and up to 59%. The benefits generalize to RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, with a geometric-mean throughput speedup of $1.28\times$ (up to $2.20\times$) over the same baseline. A capacity analysis further models and explains variation in gains and remaining gaps to CC-off serving.

title: Schism: Reconfigurable Scale-Up Domains for Distributed Quantum Computing
summary:
Switch-based quantum datacenters connect quantum processing units (QPUs) through photonic switches and shared Bell-state measurement (BSM) devices. Sharing BSMs saves hardware, but fixed connectivity constrains access to these resources. Local communication can overload one rack's BSMs while others remain idle; reaching those idle resources incurs additional optical loss and retries through switches and quantum frequency converters (QFCs). Programs remain locked into this locality-contention tradeoff as their communication patterns change.
  We propose Schism, an architecture that lets programs dynamically change which QPUs share each BSM pool. Schism places BSM pools at aggregation switches and QFCs on their core-facing uplinks. Top-of-rack switches establish reconfigurable native-wavelength circuits from QPUs to these pools, forming scale-up domains bounded by the optical loss budget. Reconfiguration reshapes resource sharing across racks without moving QPUs or migrating quantum states. Our key insight is that QPU grouping jointly determines photon-path loss and contention for BSM resources: locality alone cannot identify the best grouping, and a grouping pays off only if its savings outweigh the delay of reconfiguring to it. We develop an optimization framework that combines graph partitioning with resource-constrained completion-time estimates and dynamic programming to select how QPUs share BSM pools and when those groupings reconfigure, between or within circuit phases.
  Our evaluation using SeQUeNCe with trapped-ion parameters shows that Schism achieves communication speedups of 4.9-7.3x across 11 workloads on 32 QPUs compared to Fixed Clos connectivity and 3.6-8.3x compared to SwitchQNet. Schism also outperforms a hypothetical network-wide switch by 1.35-1.38x on the eight workloads whose phases fit in a pool, and trails it by 1.1-1.75x on the other three.

title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
summary: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

title: Two Rounds Are Already Hard for Loop-Free Updates of Routing Trees
summary: Updating a routing tree can create loops even when the old and new trees lead to the same destination. A controller chooses which routers update in each round, but their updates may finish in any order. Strong loop freedom therefore requires every partial completion to be acyclic. We show that deciding whether two rounds suffice is NP-complete, even when a safe three-round schedule is supplied. The proof is a linear-size reduction from 3-SAT with one old clause spine and four routers per variable. Three types of mixed cycles enforce consistent literal choices and clause satisfaction. For every nonempty input formula, the constructed instance needs exactly two rounds if the formula is satisfiable and exactly three otherwise.

title: Measuring GPU Memory Traffic on the NVIDIA GB10 Without C2C Telemetry
summary: The NVIDIA GB10, used in the DGX Spark and in desktop AI systems from several vendors, joins an Arm CPU die and a Blackwell GPU die with NVLink C2C. The GPU has no local memory, so every GPU access that misses in its L2 cache crosses C2C to the LPDDR5X attached to the CPU die. Yet the software on the systems we tested exposes no counter for this traffic. We show that five L2 sector counters of the GPU, sampled every 10 ms through NVIDIA's CUPTI sampling interface by a process that does not attach to the workload, measure GPU memory traffic live and separate copy engine traffic from the read misses and writes of GPU kernels. For large streaming transfers of known size, the counters agree within 0.28% on an Acer GN100 and within 0.005% on a DGX Spark, track the volume moved regardless of how it is split into copies, and exclude data reused in L2. The GPU's SMMU counter, a natural alternative, counts address translations rather than bytes. Applied to an unmodified server, the method shows Mistral 7B decode reading 13.47 GiB per token, the weights it uses plus its key value (KV) cache, at 83% of the memory bandwidth NVIDIA specifies. We release the method as an open source tool.

title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
comment: 49 pages (19 pp. main text & refs, Appendices A-F from p. 20), 23 numbered figures (24 graphic files), 13 numbered tables. Unified formal theory of the sparse node-anchored hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m), superseding arXiv:2410.00583v1. Lean 4 mechanization: https://github.com/Tongji708A/hsfn-lean (49 modules, 853 kernel-audited statements, zero sorry, commit 664b9d7)
summary: Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.
